claim: µGUIDE is a general Bayesian framework to estimate posterior distributions of tissue microstructure parameters from any given biophysical model or signal representation.
source: This work proposes µGUIDE: a general Bayesian framework to estimate posterior distributions of tissue microstructure parameters from any given biophysical model or signal representation, with exemplar demonstration in diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as the main contribution of the work

claim: µGUIDE harnesses a new deep learning architecture for automatic signal feature selection combined with simulation-based inference and efficient sampling of the posterior distributions.
source: Harnessing a new deep learning architecture for automatic signal feature selection combined with simulation-based inference and efficient sampling of the posterior distributions, µGUIDE bypasses the high computational and time cost of conventional Bayesian approaches and does not rely on acquisition constraints to define model-specific summary statistics.
evidence: Described in the abstract as a methodological feature

claim: µGUIDE bypasses the high computational and time cost of conventional Bayesian approaches.
source: Harnessing a new deep learning architecture for automatic signal feature selection combined with simulation-based inference and efficient sampling of the posterior distributions, µGUIDE bypasses the high computational and time cost of conventional Bayesian approaches and does not rely on acquisition constraints to define model-specific summary statistics.
evidence: Stated as a benefit in the abstract and demonstrated through timing comparisons with MCMC

claim: µGUIDE does not rely on acquisition constraints to define model-specific summary statistics.
source: Harnessing a new deep learning architecture for automatic signal feature selection combined with simulation-based inference and efficient sampling of the posterior distributions, µGUIDE bypasses the high computational and time cost of conventional Bayesian approaches and does not rely on acquisition constraints to define model-specific summary statistics.
evidence: Stated as a methodological advantage in the abstract

claim: The posterior distributions obtained by µGUIDE allow to highlight degeneracies present in the model definition.
source: The obtained posterior distributions allow to highlight degeneracies present in the model definition and quantify the uncertainty and ambiguity of the estimated parameters.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and demonstrated in results section

claim: The posterior distributions obtained by µGUIDE quantify the uncertainty and ambiguity of the estimated parameters.
source: The obtained posterior distributions allow to highlight degeneracies present in the model definition and quantify the uncertainty and ambiguity of the estimated parameters.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and demonstrated through uncertainty and ambiguity measures

claim: Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is a promising technique for characterizing brain microstructure in vivo using a paradigm called microstructure imaging.
source: Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is a promising technique for characterizing brain microstructure in vivo using a paradigm called microstructure imaging (Novikov et al., 2019; Alexander et al., 2019; Jelescu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature

claim: Microstructure imaging quantifies histologically meaningful features of brain microstructure by fitting a forward (biophysical) model voxel-wise to the set of signals obtained from images acquired with different sensitivities.
source: Traditionally, microstructure imaging quantifies histologically meaningful features of brain microstructure by fitting a forward (biophysical) model voxel-wise to the set of signals obtained from images acquired with different sensitivities, yielding model parameter maps (Alexander et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to established methodology

claim: Most commonly used techniques rely on a non-linear curve fitting of the signal and return the optimal solution.
source: Most commonly used techniques rely on a non-linear curve fitting of the signal and return the optimal solution, that is the best parameters guess of the fitting procedure.
evidence: Describes current standard practice in the field

claim: Non-linear curve fitting may hide model degeneracy, that is all the other possible estimates that could explain the observed signal equally well.
source: However, this may hide model degeneracy, that is all the other possible estimates that could explain the observed signal equally well (Jelescu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on model degeneracy

claim: Accounting for uncertainty in parameter estimates serves various purposes, including assessing result confidence, quantifying noise effects, or assisting in experimental design.
source: This uncertainty serves various purposes, including assessing result confidence (Jones, 2003), quantifying noise effects (Behrens et al., 2003), or assisting in experimental design (Alexander, 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: A large number of studies have focused on attempting to remove degeneracies in microstructure imaging.
source: Instead of attempting to remove the degeneracies, which has been the focus of a large number of studies (Palombo et al., 2023; de Almeida Martins et al., 2021; Slator et al., 2021; Jelescu et al., 2022; Warner et al., 2023; Uhl et al., 2024; Mougel et al., 2024; Olesen et al., 2022; Palombo et al., 2020; Howard et al., 2022; Jones et al., 2018; Vincent et al., 2020; Henriques et al., 2021; Afzali et al., 2021; Lampinen et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2012; Guerreri et al., 2023; Gyori et al., 2022; Novikov et al., 2018), we propose to highlight them and present all the possible parameter values that could explain an observed signal, providing users with more information to make more confident and explainable use of the inference results.
evidence: Supported by extensive citations to prior work

claim: Posterior distributions are powerful tools to characterize all the possible parameter estimations that could explain an observed measurement, their uncertainty, and existing model degeneracy.
source: Posterior distributions are powerful tools to characterize all the possible parameter estimations that could explain an observed measurement, their uncertainty, and existing model degeneracy (Box and Tiao, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bayesian statistics literature
